strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and timely question—whether LLMs possess human-like inductive biases toward efficient semantic compression—with a well-motivated, theory-driven framework (Information Bottleneck) from cognitive science.

The methodological design is clever: adapting iterated language learning into an iterated in-context language learning (IICLL) paradigm with pseudowords is a sensible way to probe implicit inductive biases while mitigating the confound of direct imitation of training data.

Replicating two influential human behavioral studies (English color naming; Xu et al.'s iterated learning chains) provides a clear empirical anchor for comparing LLM behavior to human data, with multiple complementary evaluation measures (efficiency loss, IB-alignment, human-alignment).

Careful experimental controls are present in places: text vs. image input conditions, multiple random seeds, random initialization with varying category counts, and an imperceptible-noise robustness check.
weaknesses: The paper is very short (4 pages of content) and underdeveloped for a top-tier venue: key methodological details are missing, including how the counterfactual 'strong baseline of hypothetical variants' is constructed, how IB-alignment and human-alignment are formally computed, how many IICLL chains/generations were run, and how prompt sensitivity was handled. There is no mention of code or data release, limiting reproducibility.

Scope is narrow: only two LLMs and a single semantic domain (color). Claims that 'LLMs are capable of evolving perceptually grounded, human-like semantic systems' generalize far beyond the evidence; a broader model sweep or additional domains would be needed to support conclusions about LLMs in general.

The central claim that LLM results are 'not simply mimicry' of training data is not fully established. Pseudowords reduce lexical imitation, but LLMs have certainly encountered textual descriptions of WCS/English color naming statistics (e.g., RGB values, color category discussions) during pretraining; no experiment directly disentangles an intrinsic efficiency bias from learned color-partition priors.

Several quantitative comparisons lack statistical rigor: no significance tests or effect sizes for differences between models (e.g., Gemini vs. Llama efficiency loss) or between LLM convergence and human/WCS baselines; only 10 seeds with STDs reported.

Manuscript quality issues undermine polish: a broken citation '[? ]' appears twice in critical positions, a typo in the section title ('Introduton'), and Figure 1 is dense and difficult to parse, with key quantitative results relegated to small panels.

The interpretation of why Gemini-img vs. Gemini-txt differ is speculative ('one possibility is...'), and the claimed role of model size is confounded—Llama 3.3-70B differs from Gemini 2.0-flash in training data, alignment procedure, and multimodality, not just size.

strengths: The research question is interesting and cognitively well-motivated: testing whether LLMs exhibit an inductive bias toward IB-efficient semantic systems, extending the theoretical framework of Zaslavsky et al. (2018) to LLMs.

The use of pseudowords in the iterated in-context language learning (IICLL) experiment is a thoughtful design choice to mitigate the confound that LLMs simply mimic real color terms seen in training data.

The study replicates two established human behavioral paradigms (English color naming and iterated language learning), enabling direct comparison with human data through a principled theoretical lens (IB bound).
Results are reported over multiple random seeds with standard deviations, and a robustness check with imperceptible input noise is included.
The comparison of textual (RGB) vs. image-based color input in the multimodal model is an interesting manipulation that yields suggestive findings about input representation effects.
weaknesses: Insufficient methodological detail for reproducibility or evaluation: the IICLL setup (number of chains, generations, sample sizes per generation, prompting details, how the full 330-color naming task is elicited) is not specified; the three evaluation measures (efficiency loss, IB-alignment, human-alignment) are never formally defined; and the 'strong counterfactual baseline of hypothetical variants' is mentioned but never described or quantified. No code or data release is indicated.

The central causal claim is overreached: the paper concludes that LLMs are 'driven by the same fundamental principle' (IB efficiency) and are 'intrinsically guided by a drive toward IB-efficiency,' but convergence toward efficient systems in iterated learning could arise from generic regularization/generalization pressures or residual training-data influence (e.g., via the structure of the English terms used in the naming task), and the paper does not rule this out. The claim that systems are 'perceptually grounded' is also not established.

Very limited model coverage: only two LLMs (one proprietary, one 70B open-weights) are tested, justified by the demands of the IICLL task. This severely limits the generality of claims about 'LLMs' as a class, and the model-size/complexity conjecture is based on a single pair of models and remains speculative.

Statistical support is weak: no significance tests or effect sizes are reported for key comparisons (e.g., Gemini vs. English alignment, LLM vs. human ILL trends, efficiency loss across generations); conclusions rest largely on visual inspection of Figure 1 curves and a small table of means.

Evidence of a rushed or incomplete manuscript: there is a broken citation ('[? ]' twice, referring to the I-ICL framework the method is built on), a typo in the section heading ('Introducton'), and the paper is very short (roughly 3 pages of content), leaving no room for analysis, discussion of limitations, or related work on LLMs and semantic categorization.

Missing analyses that would substantially strengthen the contribution: no qualitative analysis of the evolved category structures (e.g., which categories emerge, whether they match typologically common partitions), no analysis of naming variability or consistency across seeds, and no exploration of how prompt phrasing or sampling temperature affects the trajectories.

The claim that Gemini 'achieves a significantly high IB-efficiency score' relative to human English speakers is not clearly supported; efficiency-loss values in Table 1 are higher for Gemini than Llama, and the framing of which model 'aligns well' is inconsistent between the abstract and the results.

strengths: Cognitively motivated and well-grounded research question: probing whether LLMs possess an inductive bias toward IB-efficient semantic systems, rather than merely mimicking training data, is a clear and interesting question that connects LLM research with cognitive science and semantic typology.

Solid theoretical framing: the paper builds on a well-established IB framework [11] with strong empirical support across languages, and evaluation measures (efficiency loss, IB-alignment, human-alignment) are principled and directly derived from the theory.

Novel and appropriate methodology: extending iterated in-context learning to iterated in-context *language* learning (IICLL) with pseudowords is a clever way to decouple the models' behavior from memorized lexical patterns, and the multi-generation, multi-initialization design (k ∈ {2,...,14}) mirrors the human iterated learning literature faithfully.

Useful controls: testing both textual RGB and image-patch input representations, running multiple random seeds (10), and including an imperceptible-noise robustness check strengthen the Bearer [REDACTED] naming result.

The central qualitative findings—convergence toward the IB bound and toward human/WCS-like systems over generations—are interesting and potentially impactful for work on human-LLM alignment and learned inductive biases.
weaknesses: Evaluation is thin and compressed: the entire experimental evidence is a single figure and one table. There are no statistical significance tests reported for the central claims (e.g., that efficiency loss and alignment improve beyond the stated 'counterfactual baseline'), and the baseline itself is described qualitatively ('above and beyond a strong counterfactual baseline of hypothetical variants') but its construction and quantitative results are never presented. This leaves the strongest claim under-supported.

Very limited model coverage: only two LLMs (one proprietary, one open-weights), justified by task difficulty. Claims about 'LLMs' generally and about model size as a factor rest on a single Llama model with no smaller/larger open-weights comparisons or other model families; the size-complexity hypothesis is speculative.

The central mechanistic claim—that convergence reflects an intrinsic bias toward IB-efficiency rather than some other inductive bias—is not definitively established. Convergence to regular, well-partitioned systems under iterated learning is also predicted by many general prior-bias accounts (e.g., smoothing/regularization, prior over category structures); the paper does not run the control experiments needed to isolate the IB drive specifically.

Key methodological details are missing or broken: there is a literal broken citation ('[? ]') for the I-ICL framework the method builds on; details of prompt construction, sampling, generation counts, how complexity range differences between models were analyzed, and how the structural-similarity (alignment) metrics are computed are not provided, which limits reproducibility. No code/data release is mentioned.

Scope of conclusions exceeds the evidence: claims about 'perceptually grounded' semantic systems are questionable for the text-RGB condition, where no perception is involved; and the color domain, while a classic testbed, is one narrow domain—the conclusions generalize far beyond what was tested.

Presentation issues: typos in the title of the introduction ('Introduton'), a citation rendering error in Section 3.2, and a 4-page main body suggest the paper is underdeveloped for a full conference submission; figures are dense and hard to parse without more supporting quantitative detail (e.g., per-generation trajectories per condition, CIs on the information plane).

strengths: Strong conceptual framing: the paper connects the Information Bottleneck account of semantic efficiency (Zaslavsky et al., 2018) with iterated language learning to ask whether LLMs possess a human-like inductive bias toward efficient categorization, a genuinely interesting and well-motivated question that goes beyond prior work (e.g., Marjieh et al., 2024) that only tested whether LLMs can recover color naming systems.

Comprehensive and careful empirical design: 39 models across 6 families spanning size, instruction-tuning, modality, and training checkpoints (Olmo 2), with both text (sRGB, CIELAB) and image-based stimulus presentation, enabling systematic conclusions about which model properties matter.

Novel methodological contribution (IICLL): extending I-ICL to iterated in-context language learning is a sensible, well-executed way to simulate cultural transmission in LLMs while closely matching the human experiment of Xu et al. (2013), enabling direct quantitative comparison to human IL chains and WCS languages.

Rigorous analysis and controls: efficiency loss and NID-based alignment metrics grounded in prior literature, rotation analysis showing emergent Gemini systems are nontrivially aligned to human color organization, a nearest-neighbor baseline showing Gemini's results exceed simple feature clustering, sanity checks on training-data recovery, window-size ablations, and supplementary IICLL with smaller models confirming capability constraints.

Findings are informative and nuanced: the dissociation between English-alignment and general human (WCS) alignment in some models, the complexity cutoff for multimodal benefit, the training-trajectory analysis, and the observation that only the strongest in-context model recapitulates the full range of human IB tradeoffs are all substantive results.
Good reproducibility practices: full model list with IDs, example prompts, stated plans to release code, and reliance on publicly available WCS data and the published IB model.
weaknesses: The central claim that IICLL reveals an intrinsic 'inductive bias toward IB-efficiency' rather than training-data mimicry is not fully airtight: pseudo-words mitigate direct lexical mimicry, but the model's representation of the color space and notions of 'good' category structure could still derive from exposure to human color-naming patterns, so the human-likeness of the emergent systems may partly reflect training data at the level of perceptual structure rather than a generic efficiency bias. The paper acknowledges but does not fully resolve this.

Key positive results (full range of near-optimal IB tradeoffs, rotation analysis significance, Shepard circles generalization) rest disproportionately on a single closed-source model (Gemini 2.0), limiting generality and raising concerns about reproducibility and API versioning; the other tested frontier-scale models converge to low-complexity solutions.

Some important details feel under-specified or post hoc: the sliding-window history mechanism (a deviation from the human experiment whose impact is 'crudely' motivated), the selective reporting of the k=14 condition where only Gemini sometimes passed the sanity threshold, and reliance on different decoding methods (controlled generation vs. log-prob scoring) across models.

Primarily an empirical, cognitive-science-flavored contribution; there is no theoretical or mechanistic account of why or how the efficiency bias emerges in LLMs, which the authors themselves flag as future work. Impact may be strongest in the cognitive-science/emergent-communication sub-area rather than core AI.

Minor presentation issues: several typos ('paradign', 'an minimal pair', 'that are efficient that their rotated counterparts'), inconsistent notation, and some figures (e.g., Figure 9 mode maps) are dense and hard to read.
The Shepard circles extension is a preliminary, single-model, qualitative exploration; as evidence for domain-generality it is suggestive but thin.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical scope: testing 39 models across 6 families (varying size, instruction-tuning, modality, and even training checkpoints for OLMo 2) is a substantial effort that goes well beyond prior work (e.g., Marjieh et al., 2024), and enables meaningful conclusions about scaling and training-stage effects on color naming.

Methodologically interesting extension: Iterated in-Context Language Learning (IICLL) is a clever prompt-based adaptation of iterated learning that closely replicates the Xu et al. (2013) human experiment, allowing a direct human-LLM comparison of inductive biases.

Theoretically grounded evaluation: the use of the IB framework with efficiency loss, NID-based alignment measures, and the theoretical bound from Zaslavsky et al. (2018) gives the analysis quantitative rigor rather than purely qualitative claims.

Thoughtful control analyses: the rotation analysis (Appendix H) to rule out arbitrary efficiency, the nearest-neighbor baseline (Appendix M) to rule out trivial feature clustering, sanity checks on ICL retrieval, and ablations over conversation-window size strengthen the interpretation of the IICLL results.

The paper is generally well written and well positioned relative to the cognitive science and emergent communication literatures, and the reproducibility statement plus appendices with prompts and model IDs are commendable.
weaknesses: Limited novelty over closely related work: the core ingredients (LLM color naming via hex/RGB prompting, IB analysis of lexicons, iterated learning with LLMs) all exist in prior papers the authors themselves cite (Marjieh et al., 2024; Zhu & Griffiths, 2024; Carlsson et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2024). The contribution is largely an incremental combination and scaling of these elements rather than a new method or conceptual insight.

The central claim that LLMs exhibit a 'human-like inductive bias toward IB-efficiency' is stronger than the evidence supports. The IICLL results are confounded by in-context capability: the only model reproducing the full human tradeoff range (Gemini 2.0) is also the model with the strongest ICL abilities, and the authors concede that models without strong ICL collapse to low-complexity solutions. Convergence to simple, structured partitions under data compression pressure may reflect generic model behavior (or even generic ICL compression), not a specifically human-like or color-specific bias.

Narrow domain generality: the Shepard circles experiment (Section 4.3) is a small, single-model, preliminary result with no efficiency or alignment analysis comparable to the color study, yet it is used to support broad claims about domain-general inductive biases. One frontier model and qualitative mode maps are insufficient for that inference.

Evaluation fairness concerns for the English naming task: constraining models to 14 terms and to raw sRGB/CIELAB coordinate inputs is a harsh testbed that most LLMs would rarely see in this form during training; the finding that most models 'fail' may partly reflect interface mismatch rather than lack of color knowledge, especially since performance degrades with CIELAB input and improves when the prompt hints that coordinates are sRGB (Appendix F). The paper does not fully disentangle representation from encoding artifacts.

Dependence on closed, non-reproducible APIs: the headline result rests on Gemini 2.0, a proprietary model whose versions and behavior can change, undermining reproducibility and the stability of the claims over time. The claim that only the frontier model passes the threshold is effectively unverifiable and may become outdated quickly.

Statistical rigor is uneven: IICLL results are averaged across initializations with 95% CIs assuming normality, but the number of chains per condition and per model, and formal significance tests comparing LLM trajectories against human IL data, are not clearly reported; the rotation-analysis significance claims are similarly underspecified.

Some interpretive inconsistencies: the paper is at pains to show LLMs fail to recover English color naming yet simultaneously argues this implies human-like semantic structure (via WCS-like low-resource languages), and the sliding conversation window is an ad hoc addition that departs from the human experiment it claims to replicate, potentially introducing recency effects that shape the emergent systems.

Practical significance is unclear: beyond a demonstration that the largest models approximate the IB bound on one domain, the paper offers limited guidance on why this matters for AI systems or what actionable insight follows, and the discussion of mechanisms (training data, instruction tuning, model size) is deferred to future work.

strengths: The paper makes a well-motivated and novel contribution by combining two theoretically grounded frameworks (Information Bottleneck efficiency and iterated language learning) to ask whether LLMs possess human-like inductive biases toward semantic efficiency, going beyond prior work that merely tested color-term recovery from prompts (e.g., Marjieh et al., 2024).

The methodology is carefully designed to replicate influential human experiments (Lindsey & Brown, 2014; Xu et al., 2013) as closely as possible, enabling direct quantitative comparison of LLM behavior against human data on the IB information plane, including the rotation analysis of Regier et al. (2007).

The evaluation is broad and thorough: 39 models across 6 families varying in size, instruction tuning, and modality; both text (sRGB/CIELAB) and image-based stimuli; checkpoint analysis of OLMo 2 training dynamics; and multiple metrics (efficiency loss, NID-based alignment to English, WCS, and IB optima).

The paper includes useful control analyses that strengthen the central claim: a nearest-neighbor baseline showing Gemini's emergent systems exceed simple feature clustering, a sanity check for ICL comprehension, a sliding-window ablation, and supplementary IICLL runs with smaller models that cleanly demonstrate a capability threshold.

The introduction of IICLL is a simple but elegant extension of I-ICL (Zhu & Griffiths, 2024) that enables simulation of cultural transmission of language in LLMs, and the finding that only the strongest in-context model recapitulates the full range of human IB tradeoffs is an interesting, informative result.
Reproducibility is addressed thoughtfully: model IDs, prompts (Appendix J), procedure details, and a commitment to release code; human and typological datasets are publicly available or attributable.
weaknesses: The headline claim that LLMs exhibit a 'human-like inductive bias toward IB-efficiency' rests largely on one closed-source model (Gemini 2.0) whose training data and inference details are opaque; the generality and mechanistic basis of the claimed bias remain unclear, as the authors themselves acknowledge.

Results are sensitive to prompting and encoding choices: performance degrades substantially with CIELAB inputs, the sRGB 'hint' changed OLMo behavior, and API-specific decoding (controlled generation for Gemini vs. log-prob scoring for open models) introduces potential confounds across model comparisons that are not fully disentangled.

The 'not merely mimicking training data' argument is indirect: the IICLL stimuli are presented as abstract 'features', but sRGB-encoded color triples plausibly appear with color-term associations online, and a stronger de-identification or counterfactual control (e.g., permuted feature spaces) is only partially addressed (NN baseline covers contiguity but not all mimicry concerns).

The Shepard circles experiment is a preliminary, single-model, single-visualization analysis (Figure 5b) with no quantitative evaluation, yet it is used to support claims of a 'domain-general' bias; this part of the paper is significantly under-supported relative to the rest.

Some statistical reporting is thin: confidence intervals are shown for aggregate curves, but key comparative claims (e.g., Gemini vs. human IL chains, cutoff at ~3 bits complexity) lack formal significance tests, and the number of IICLL chain replicates per condition in the main analyses is not clearly stated.

The stochastic encoders used for evaluation require multiple responses per chip, but the sampling procedure and number of repetitions per stimulus are not documented in the main text or appendices, which affects reproducibility of the mutual-information estimates.

Positioning relative to the closest prior work (Carlsson et al., 2024, which showed IB-efficient color naming via iterated learning + communication in neural agents) could be sharper; the increment is the use of LLMs and ICL, which is clear, but the theoretical novelty is moderate.
